«Большевики пишут письмо Чемберлену» / «.finding: In ch. 5 Bender considers offering the Stargorod children's commission (Стардеткомиссия) the rights to a still-unpainted picture, 'The Bolsheviks Write a Letter to Chamberlain', modelled on Repin's 'Zaporozhian Cossacks Write a Letter to the Sultan' (Russian Museum, 1880–91; English title 'Reply of the Zaporozhian Cossacks'), which every Russian knew: a crowd of laughing Cossacks dictating an obscene refusal to the Turkish sultan's demand of submission. The joke is topical: on 23 Feb 1927 British Foreign Secretary Austen Chamberlain sent a note demanding the USSR stop anti-British propaganda; Pravda answered with 'Our answer to Chamberlain' (2 Mar 1927), Britain broke off relations in May after the ARCOS raid, and the slogan became a nationwide poster/fund-raising campaign (Osoaviakhim air squadron 'Our answer to Chamberlain'), so Chamberlain was the stock villain of 1927 cartoons. Bender's idea is even second-hand: Krasny Perets no. 6 (1923) had already printed 'The Bolsheviks Write a Reply to the English Curzon' with Kalinin, Chicherin, Trotsky, Stalin etc. in the Cossacks' poses. Kalinin (head of state, 'all-Union elder') and Chicherin (foreign commissar) are the leaders whose costumes Bender worries about; the phrase 'наш ответ Чемберлену' survives in Russian as an ironic idiom for a blustering 'worthy reply'. The Richardson English translation renders it 'The Bolsheviks Answer Chamberlain' after 'The Zaporozhe Cossacks Answer the Sultan'.

«Быстроупак».finding: «Быстроупак» is a fictional private packing office in Stargorod: in chapter X it 'announces itself to respected citizen-customers with a black sign with round gold letters' next to the bagel artel, its 'молодцы' (toughs) help the militiaman and later queue for flour, and in chapter XIV its owner Дядьев, a former textile merchant and NEP businessman, is fleeced by Bender's 'Union of the Sword and Ploughshare'. The name is a mock Soviet-style clipped compound (быстро + упаковка), the same pattern as real 1920s abbreviations (Хлебопродукт, Москвошвея), and Ilf recorded it in his 1927 notebook simply as 'Упаковочная контора «Быстроупак»' alongside 'Пивная «Вавилон»', i.e. as a specimen of absurd NEP-era shop names. For a Russian reader it connotes a small private nepman firm dressed in bureaucratic-sounding branding; it is not a proverbial phrase. John Richardson's English translation (1961, the standard text online) renders it 'Fastpack' throughout ('the Fastpack packing office', 'young toughs from Fastpack', 'Dyadyev, owner of Fastpack'). Search did not surface the Chinese (张佩文 2004; 白桦熊 2022) or Japanese (江川卓 1969) renderings; those are not verified.

«Коль славен наш господь в Сионе».finding: Bortniansky's hymn (1794, words by Kheraskov, after a psalm), used as the unofficial state anthem of the Russian Empire before 'Боже, Царя храни' (1833), and thereafter still the tune the Kremlin's Spasskaya Tower chimes played from 1856 until October 1917; it was then the official hymn of the White armies (1918–23) and of the émigré community. For a Soviet reader in 1928 it was therefore not a random church piece but the sound of the old regime and the Whites, which is why a NEP-era fire extinguisher 'Эклер' hissing this melody (Chapter VIII, the old women's home) is a joke of misplaced loyalties. Sources give no Soviet ban, but the association with tsarism and emigration was live. Established renderings: English 'How Glorious Is Our Lord in Zion' (en.wikipedia, recordings); Chinese 吾主在锡安是何等光荣 (zh.wikipedia article title); Japanese has no article of its own — the Bortniansky page uses the transliteration 『コリ・スラーヴェン』 and Russia Beyond uses 「シオンのわれらが主の何と輝かしき」. The prompt's mention of Durov/VKontakte and '2013' does not apply; the book is 1928.

«Огонек».finding: «Огонёк» (Ogonyok, 'little flame') is a real illustrated weekly magazine: founded in St Petersburg on 21 December 1899 as a supplement to Birzhevye vedomosti, closed in 1918, and refounded in Moscow on 1 April 1923 by the Pravda journalist Mikhail Koltsov, who edited it until his arrest in 1938. In the 1920s it was the mass-circulation Soviet picture weekly (photos, popular science, fiction, current events), a lowbrow-respectable magazine found in barbershops and waiting rooms; it later reached 4.6 million copies under Vitaly Korotich in the glasnost era and ceased print publication in December 2020 under Kommersant. In the novel (Part 1, ch. 2) the barber 'Pierre and Constantine', alias Andrei Ivanovich, airs his medical knowledge 'почерпнутые им из московского журнала «Огонек»', which lies on his table 'для услаждения бреющихся граждан' — the joke is a provincial barber retailing half-digested popular-science snippets as expertise. The 1961 John Richardson English translation renders it 'the Moscow magazine Ogonyok'; Chinese sources (zh.wikipedia, tsrus.cn) consistently use 《星火》; Japanese coverage is split between transliterations オゴニョーク and アガニョーク (RBTH Japan uses 「アガニョーク」（ともしび）).

rendering.ja: モスクワの絵入り週刊誌『オゴニョーク』

«Огонек».note_for_reader: Ogonyok (Огонёк, 'Little Flame'): Russia's oldest illustrated weekly, founded 1899, relaunched in Moscow in 1923 — a popular picture magazine with science and health snippets, not a medical journal.
«Огонек».rationale: Kept the denotation (a real, named magazine, transliterated in en/ja as existing translations and press do; the established Chinese calque 《星火》 kept because Chinese coverage never transliterates it) and the connotation via a brief in-text epithet 'illustrated weekly / 画报周刊 / 絵入り週刊誌' so the reader sees it is a popular picture magazine; gave up the diminutive 'little flame' image in en/ja (recovered only in the note) and, in zh, the sound of the Russian name.

слесарь-интеллигент.finding: Narrator's epithet for Viktor Mikhailovich Polesov, introduced in ch. X ('Слесарь, попугай и гадалка') at the courtyard well, filling a petrol can with water; the chapter later calls the gate fiasco 'венцом академической деятельности слесаря-интеллигента', and the fuller tag 'слесарь-интеллигент со средним образованием' / 'кустарь-одиночка с мотором' became a Russian catchphrase for the busybody who has an opinion on everything and finishes nothing. 'Слесарь' here is a metal-fitter/mechanic (he owns a workshop, builds a motorcycle from car parts, repairs gates), not a locksmith; 'интеллигент' is the social type (the educated, self-important class), so the compound is a deliberate oxymoron in the mock-solemn register of NEP job titles. Established English: Richardson (1961) 'the mechanic-intellectual'; reviewers of Fisher (2011) also write 'mechanic intellectual'. The Chinese translation's chapter title '钳工、鹦鹉和女巫' shows 钳工 is the established Chinese for слесарь; no Japanese rendering of the epithet (江川卓 1969) could be verified online.

rendering.ja: インテリ機械工

слесарь-интеллигент.note_for_reader: 'Intellectual' here is the Russian social type intelligent (the educated, opinionated class), pinned mockingly on a workshop mechanic with a secondary education who never finishes a job.
слесарь-интеллигент.rationale: Kept the oxymoronic compound and the mock-official job-title register in all three languages (Richardson's established English, 钳工 established in Chinese, インテリ the direct Japanese loan of интеллигент); gave up 'locksmith' (wrong denotation) and the 'intellectual mechanic' word order, which turns the social label into a mere adjective and loses the joke.

туды ее в качель.finding: A sub-standard folk euphemism: 'туды' is dialect for 'туда', 'качель' is Dahl's feminine singular of 'качели' (swing), so it means literally 'into the swing with it/her' and stands in for an obscene mat oath ('Словарь современной лексики, жаргона и сленга' 2014 labels it 'эвфемизм... вместо матерной брани', everyday jargon). It carries no real meaning about swings: for a Russian reader it is Bezenchuk the coffin-maker's verbal tic, spoken three times in chapter I alone ('Нимфа, туды ее в качель, разве товар дает?'), and since the 1971/1976 films it is a proverbial quotation that everyone knows and nobody analyses; amateur etymologies (a 'cellar' sense of качель) are unsupported. In the standard Richardson English translation (lib.ru text) it is flattened every time to 'durn it', which Russian readers of that translation specifically complain about as losing the colour; a Chinese e-text (zhangyue.com) renders it '去他妈的', which is cruder than the original. Anne Fisher's 2011 English, 张佩文's Chinese and 江川卓's 1969 Japanese renderings could not be verified online.

rendering.ja: ブランコにでも乗せちまえ

туды ее в качель.note_for_reader: Bezenchuk's oath, literally 'into the swing with it', is a nonsense folk euphemism for an obscene curse; it is rendered by one fixed formula throughout.
туды ее в качель.rationale: Each rendering is cast in the target language's own 'to hell with it' mould (to hell with it / 去他的 / ～ちまえ) with the swing image dropped in where hell would go, so the reader hears a familiar curse shape gone slightly absurd: register (low, non-obscene, folksy) and the fixed-tag function are kept, the literal denotation is kept only as the absurd image, and the established but colourless 'durn it' is rejected because it erases the signature.

милиционер.finding: A milítsioner is a rank-and-file officer of the milítsiya, the Soviet civil police. The name was adopted by the Provisional Government's decree of 17 April 1917 and reaffirmed by the Bolsheviks on 10 November 1917 as the 'Workers' and Peasants' Militsiya', deliberately chosen to tie the new force to popular self-organisation and to disown the tsarist 'politsiya'; the word survived until Russia restored 'politsiya' on 1 March 2011. In 1928 it therefore carried a distinctly new-regime flavour: a milítsioner is the ordinary street cop of NEP Russia, a figure of mild comedy rather than fear (the terror organs were the OGPU, not the militsiya), and the narrators use him as a stock piece of Soviet street furniture. John Richardson's English translation (the widely circulated 1961/1965 text) renders the institution as 'the Soviet militia' in explicit contrast to 'the tsarist police'; Japanese reference usage is 民警 (ミリツィヤ) for the Soviet-era force versus 警察 for post-2011; Chinese Wikipedia titles the force 苏联民兵 but records 民警 as the standard alternative, and in Chinese everyday usage 民警 also denotes an ordinary uniformed officer of the PRC's 人民警察, which makes it read naturally. The prompt's references to 2013, Durov and VKontakte do not apply to this 1928 term and were disregarded.

rendering.ja: 民警

милиционер.note_for_reader: militsiya/militiaman: the Soviet civil police, so named from 1917 to disown the tsarist 'police'; an ordinary street cop, not the secret police.
милиционер.rationale: All three keep the denotation (a Soviet, not tsarist, police officer) and the neutral register, and 'militiaman' follows the established English rendering ('militia') used by Richardson; what is given up is the connotation of a paramilitary volunteer that 'militia' has for an English reader, and in Chinese the slight anachronism that 民警 also names today's PRC officer, both handled by the one-line note.

жилотдел.finding: Жилотдел is the War-Communism-era clipped name for the жилищный отдел, the housing department of a city or district soviet executive committee (исполком): the office that, under the December 1917 SNK/NKVD decrees on municipalising housing and the 1918 Moscow-soviet rules on requisitioning dwellings and movable property, evicted or 'compacted' (уплотнение) bourgeois households and issued ордера (written orders) allocating their rooms and furniture to workers and institutions. By the SNK statute of 8 April 1920 'жилищное дело' passed to the new коммунальные отделы of the исполкомы, and with NEP and the 1921 demunicipalisation decree the separate housing departments were wound up, which is exactly what the novel records: 'жилотдел был расформирован в 1921 году и... архив слит с архивом Старкомхоза' (ch. XI); Tikhon says 'всю мебель в 1919 году увезли в жилотдел' (ch. VII), and Korobeinikov's stolen copies of its ордера are what the whole hunt runs on. For a 1928 reader the word carried the smell of 1918-21 — requisition, communal-flat 'compaction', a defunct office whose paper still decides who owns what; by 2013 it reads as a dead Soviet bureaucratic abbreviation, one of the novel's period 'sovietisms', with a faint comic note that its own sofa sits in the hall with the upholstery ruined. The gloss's claim that it occupied the girls' school is not in the canonical text (chs. VII, XI, XII checked); the text only says 'тот дом, в котором когда-то был жилотдел'. Existing English translations (Richardson 1961, and per search snippets Fisher 2011) render it 'housing division'; no published Chinese (张佩文 2004, 白桦熊 2021) or Japanese (江川卓 1969) rendering could be verified online.

rendering.ja: 住宅部

жилотдел.note_for_reader: Zhilotdel (жилищный отдел): the local soviet's housing department of 1918-21, which requisitioned 'bourgeois' flats and furniture and issued the orders allocating them; abolished under NEP in 1921, its files passed to the municipal-economy office.
жилотдел.rationale: Keeps the denotation (a specific, named, now-defunct office whose orders and archive drive the plot) by treating it as a proper institution — capitalised English with the transliteration on first occurrence, and the established 'Housing Division' of Richardson/Fisher; 处/部 mark it as a soviet executive-committee отдел rather than a modern housing office (Japanese follows the 政治部/特別部 convention for Soviet отделы). Gives up the clipped-abbreviation flavour and the War-Communism connotation of requisition, which no target word carries, so the one-line note supplies it.

церковь Фрола и Лавра.finding: The church where Father Fyodor Vostrikov is priest in the town of N (opening sentence of Chapter III: «священник церкви Фрола и Лавра, отец Федор Востриков»). It is dedicated to the 2nd-century Illyrian martyrs Florus and Laurus (Флор и Лавр, feast 18/31 August), who in Russian folk religion were the patron saints of horses; 'Фрол' is the peasant, vernacular form of the church-Slavonic 'Флор' (Tolstoy's War and Peace has the same 'лошадиный праздник Фрола и Лавра', and 'Фролов день' was the horse holiday). Such dedications were common in Russian towns (Uglich, several Moscow churches), so to a Russian reader the name signals a thoroughly ordinary small-town parish church with a rustic, horse-and-cart flavour, which sets up the comedy of its priest's get-rich schemes; the folk form, not the ecclesiastical one, carries that flavour. Existing English: Richardson (1961) 'Church of St. Frol and St. Laurence' (a hybrid; Laurus is not Laurence), Fisher (2011) reported as 'Frol and Lavr Church'; Russia Beyond's Japanese site writes the saints フロルスとラウルス / フロールとラヴル. I could not access the published Chinese (张佩文 2004) or Japanese (江川卓 1966) texts to confirm their renderings, so those remain unverified.

rendering.en: the Church of Frol and Lavr
rendering.ja: フロールとラヴル教会

церковь Фрола и Лавра.note_for_reader: Frol and Lavr: folk forms of Sts Florus and Laurus, whom Russian peasants venerated as patrons of horses; an utterly ordinary provincial church dedication.
церковь Фрола и Лавра.rationale: Keeping the Russian folk forms (Frol/Lavr, 弗罗尔/拉夫尔, フロール/ラヴル) preserves connotation and register: the provincial, horse-fair plainness that a Russian reader hears, and it matches the recent English translation and standard Russian-name transliteration in Chinese and Japanese; it gives up immediate denotation (which saints these are), which the one-line note restores, rather than using the Latin 'Florus and Laurus' that no target reader would recognise either and that sounds formal where the original is homely.

Клавдия Ивановна.finding: Klavdia Ivanovna Petukhova is Ippolit Matveevich Vorobyaninov's тёща (his late wife Marie's mother), an old provincial noblewoman in Stargorod who dies in chapter II ('Кончина мадам Петуховой') after confessing that she sewed her diamonds into the seat of one of the twelve dining-room chairs; the novel's Part Three is titled 'Сокровище мадам Петуховой'. Chapter I gives her the book's deadpan treatment: 'Ипполит Матвеевич не любил своей тещи. Клавдия Ивановна была глупа... Скупа она была до чрезвычайности... Голос у ней был такой силы и густоты, что ему позавидовал бы Ричард Львиное Сердце', and she is a dreamer of prophetic dreams. The text calls her only 'Клавдия Ивановна', 'теща', 'старуха' or 'мадам Петухова'; the name-plus-patronymic is the ordinary respectful Russian address for an older woman and carries no joke of its own — the comedy is in the narration around her. For a Russian reader she is the stock тёща of Soviet humour (the domineering mother-in-law who knows the family money) and the origin of the whole treasure hunt. The 1961 Richardson English translation (lib.ru) anglicises her as 'Claudia Ivanovna' and uses 'mother-in-law' throughout; a search summary claimed Fisher (2011) does the same but this could not be verified. The 2022 上海译文 Chinese edition (白桦熊) titles chapter II '佩图霍娃太太辞世'; 克拉夫季娅 is the 新华社 standard Chinese for Клавдия. No Japanese source giving the katakana of her name was found (Egawa Takashi's 1966/1969 translation is not online); Japanese summaries call her 義母.

rendering.zh: 克拉夫季娅·伊万诺夫娜
rendering.ja: クラヴジヤ・イヴァーノヴナ

Клавдия Ивановна.note_for_reader: Klavdia Ivanovna Petukhova: Vorobyaninov's mother-in-law (Russian тёща, wife's mother); 'Madame Petukhova' in chapter titles is the same person.
Клавдия Ивановна.rationale: Kept denotation (one fixed transliteration per language, mirroring the Cyrillic the reader sees beside it; 'теща' always rendered as mother-in-law / 岳母 / 姑 or 義母, never 'aunt') and the neutral name-and-patronymic register; gave up Richardson's anglicised 'Claudia', and accepted that the Japanese katakana is a standard transcription rather than a verified match to Egawa's text.

«Треугольник».finding: «Треугольник» is the Petersburg rubber works on the Obvodny Canal, founded 1859/60 as the Russian-American Rubber Manufactory (ТРАРМ); from 1888 it stamped its galoshes with a triangle so that illiterate buyers could recognise them, took the trade name «Треугольник» officially in 1908, and was renamed «Красный треугольник» after nationalisation (1922). It was the country's near-monopoly galosh maker, supplier to the Imperial court, and in the NEP years the rubber trust advertised heavily (Mayakovsky wrote its slogans), so for a 1928 reader the word meant one thing: galoshes. In ch. XI the swindled archivist Korobeinikov kicks his table and «подпрыгивала пепельница, сделанная на манер калоши с красной надписью «Треугольник»» — a promotional galosh-shaped ashtray, a pun on the firm's product that also fits the petty-bourgeois clutter of his room; the same brand recurs as torn «Треугольник» tyre covers in Bezenchuk's town. Richardson's English (1961) renders it plainly as 'Triangle' ('the clog-shaped ash-tray with the word "Triangle" on it', misreading калоша as clog); English sources on the factory use 'Triangle'/'Red Triangle'. I found no published Chinese or Japanese rendering of this sentence online (the prompt's mention of Durov/VKontakte/2013 is a template slip unrelated to this 1928 term).

rendering.ja: 「三角」印（三角ゴム靴工場）

«Треугольник».note_for_reader: Triangle: the Petersburg rubber works whose galoshes, stamped with a triangle, were on every Russian foot; the ashtray is its promotional souvenir.
«Треугольник».rationale: The brand is literally a triangle, so translating the name (as Richardson did) keeps the denotation and lets the galosh-shaped ashtray carry the joke in the sentence itself; the brand-marker (牌 / 印) tells zh/ja readers it is a trademark, not a shape. Given up: the Russian sound of the name and the instant 'galoshes!' recognition, which the one-line note restores.

Старгород.finding: Старгород ('Old-town', стар- + город) is the invented provincial town where Part One ('Старгородский лев') is set: Vorobyaninov's home, the site of the Second Social Security Home, the 'Союз меча и орала', the newspaper «Старгородская правда» and the tram whose first car runs on 1 May 1927 (ch. XIII: 'первый в Старгороде вагон электрического трамвая', 'старгородцы только отпускали шуточки'). For a Russian reader the name is a mock-generic, Gogolian toponym in the line of Mirgorod and of Leskov's Stargorod in «Соборяне» (ru.wikipedia lists both), i.e. 'any sleepy old provincial town', not a real place; Starobelsk (Luhansk region, visited by Ilf and Petrov for «Гудок» in 1923; Bender monument 2007/2008) is the usual real-life prototype, with Odessa and Shargorod also claimed. Existing renderings: English editions (Richardson 1961, Fisher 2011, Wikipedia) transliterate 'Stargorod' and use it attributively ('Stargorod criminal investigation department'); Japanese coverage (Egawa Taku's translation as quoted, RBTH Japan) uses スタルゴロド; but all three Chinese editions found (张佩文 2004 人民文学, 徐昌翰 2022 江苏凤凰, 白桦熊 2022 上海译文) calque it as 老城 ('第一部 老城名流' / '老城里的狮子', '来到了老城'), not 斯塔尔戈罗德. The prompt's mention of 'Durov and VKontakte' and 'around 2013' does not apply to this term.

rendering.ja: スタルゴロド

Старгород.note_for_reader: Старгород, literally 'Old Town', is an invented provincial town in the manner of Gogol's Mirgorod; English and Japanese keep the Russian sound (Stargorod / スタルゴロド), Chinese editions translate the meaning (老城).
Старгород.rationale: en and ja follow the established transliterations of every existing translation (denotation and proper-name status kept, the 'Old Town' pun given up and supplied once in the note); zh follows the calque used by all three published Chinese translations, which keeps the meaning and mock-generic flavour at the cost of a name that looks like a common noun. Derived forms bind mechanically: старгородцы = Stargorod residents / 老城人 / スタルゴロドの住民, «Старгородская правда» = the Stargorod Pravda / 《老城真理报》 / 『スタルゴロド・プラウダ』, старгородский трамвай = the Stargorod tram / 老城电车 / スタルゴロドの市電.

Виктор Михайлович Полесов.finding: A fictional character, not a historical person: the Stargorod 'слесарь-интеллигент' introduced in chapter X ('Слесарь, попугай и гадалка'), the clumsiest of the town's 'кустари с мотором' (licensed one-man artisans of the NEP years), a 'кипучий лентяй' who abandons every job (the dismantled gate of house no. 5, a home-made motorcycle that runs once and explodes) to meddle in everyone else's, and the monarchist gossip who leads Vorobyaninov to the fortune-teller Elena Stanislavovna and is enrolled by Bender in the sham 'Union of the Sword and Ploughshare'. In the source he is named by surname, by name-patronymic, by full name, and by mocking epithets (слесарь-интеллигент, слесарь-механик, слесарь-энтузиаст, 'Витька-слесарь', 'семибатюшная гадюка со средним образованием'). For a Russian reader by 2013 'Полесов' and 'кипучий лентяй' are bywords for the frantic, opinionated busybody who is useless at his own trade; bloggers still use the name that way (2012, 2016). English coverage: Richardson's 1961 translation spells him 'Victor Mikhailovich Polesov' ('the mechanic-intellectual'); Fisher's 2011 Northwestern translation 'Viktor Mikhailovich Polesov'. Search did not surface the Chinese (张佩文 2004, 白桦熊 2021) or Japanese (江川卓 1966/1969) renderings of his name; only the Chinese chapter title '钳工、鹦鹉和算命婆' was confirmed.

rendering.ja: ヴィクトル・ミハイロヴィチ・ポレソフ

Виктор Михайлович Полесов.note_for_reader: Polesov, the 'mechanic-intellectual': a self-employed Stargorod artisan who talks like an engineer and finishes nothing; Russians still call such a man 'a Polesov'.
Виктор Михайлович Полесов.rationale: The name is kept as a plain transliteration in all three languages (Fisher's 'Viktor' over Richardson's 'Victor', standard 新华社-style and katakana forms), so every surname, name-patronymic and epithet form resolves to one visible person; the connotation of the busybody type is carried by the epithets in the running text and one note, not by the name.

Елена Станиславовна.finding: Elena Stanislavovna Bour, a fictional character: widow of a provincial prosecutor, Vorobyaninov's mistress of 1899 (he took her to Paris), now in 1927 a shabby, suspicious old woman who reads cards and palms for fifty kopecks in Stargorod, keeps a white parrot in red underpants, and hosts the 'Union of the Sword and Ploughshare' that Bender improvises around her table (chapter X 'Слесарь, попугай и гадалка', chapter XIV). Her patronymic marks a Polish father (Stanisław), a common marker of faded provincial gentility; the narration keeps her former-belle past against her present squalor, and гадалка is a plain, slightly disreputable trade word, not 'witch'. Richardson's 1961 English (lib.ru) has 'Elena Stanislavovna' and 'fortune-teller' ('The Mechanic, the Parrot and the Fortune-Teller'); a Chinese edition (AnyFlip scan) titles the chapter '钳工、鹦鹉和算命婆' and spells her 叶列娜·斯塔尼斯拉沃芙娜 (older style), while the 新华社 standard form is 叶莲娜·斯坦尼斯拉沃夫娜. Egawa Taku's Japanese (1966/1969) exists but its spelling of her name could not be checked online.

Елена Станиславовна.note_for_reader: Elena Stanislavovna: Vorobyaninov's old flame, now a card-and-palm fortune-teller; 'Stanislavovna' = daughter of Stanisław, a Polish name.
Елена Станиславовна.rationale: Keeps denotation (name + patronymic, transliterated by each language's standard system, and гадалка always as fortune-teller/占卜师/占い師, never witch or 算命婆) and the mock-solemn register; gives up the Polish-gentility connotation of the patronymic, which only the one-line note can carry.

«Сделал свое дело — и уходи».finding: It is the curt placard (плакат/лозунг) in the Stargorod ZAGS where Vorobyaninov clerks (Part I, ch. 1): the office clock hangs 'над лозунгом «Сделал свое дело — и уходи»', and a few lines later the groom in the quilted jacket is cowed by the ink smell, the wheezing clock 'а в особенности строгим плакатом «Сделал свое дело — и уходи»'; the joke follows at once: 'Хотя дела своего мужчина в пиджаке еще и не начинал, но уйти ему уже хотелось' (ZiF 1928 text; later editions 'Молодой человек еще и не начинал своего дела, а уйти ему уже хотелось'). Such peremptory notices were real fixtures of early-Soviet offices, not the authors' invention: Ilf and Petrov's 1932 feuilleton titled 'Сделал свое дело и уходи' (Советское искусство, 2 Feb 1932) catalogues them alongside 'Без дела не входить', 'Не задавай кассиру вопросов', 'Соблюдай очередь', praising their 'молодецкая безапелляционная форма'. To a Russian reader the line carries the bullying tone of petty officialdom toward the visitor (посетитель), and the novel's use made it a quotable tag. The only established published English rendering found is Richardson (1961): 'Finish Your Business and Leave', used identically at both occurrences; Fisher's 2011 wording could not be checked online. No Chinese (张佩文 et al.) or Japanese (江川卓, 1969) text of the passage is online, so those renderings are not attested. (The prompt's reference to Durov/VKontakte and 2013 does not apply to this 1928 term and was ignored.)

«Сделал свое дело — и уходи».note_for_reader: A real curt notice of 1920s Soviet offices; Ilf and Petrov later titled a 1932 feuilleton on such placards with these very words.
«Сделал свое дело — и уходи».rationale: All three keep the denotation (done = go), placard brevity, and a noun that can be reused for the pun (business/事/用 = the groom's errand) and a verb echoed by 'wanted to leave'; en adopts Richardson's established wording rather than the proposed 'State your business and go', which shifts the sense to 'before' instead of 'after'; ja uses notice-style 〜こと, giving up the personal imperative for the flat bureaucratic register; the sneering official tone is only partly carried and left to the note.

субботники.finding: A subbotnik (from суббота, 'Saturday') is a day of unpaid, nominally voluntary collective labour outside working hours. The first one was held on 12 April 1919 at the Moscow-Sortirovochnaya depot of the Moscow-Kazan railway, where fifteen workers stayed on after their shift to repair locomotives; Lenin's pamphlet 'The Great Initiative' (June 1919) called it 'the actual beginning of communism', and the first All-Russian subbotnik on 1 May 1920, with Lenin carrying logs in the Kremlin, turned it into a mass propaganda institution. In the early 1920s subbotniks were still largely a Party/Komsomol affair of the enthusiastic and the 'sympathizers'; by 1928 the word already carried the flavour of Civil-War-era zeal that NEP-era citizens remembered with a mixture of nostalgia and weariness, and it was drifting toward the later 'voluntary-compulsory' sense. In the novel it appears in three registers: as an official street name ('Alexandrovsky, now Proletarian Subbotniks, Boulevard', ch. VIII), in the engineer Treukhov's memory of 1920, when depot and rope-works men marched to the Gusishche with a band and dug holes all day for a tram line that was never built (ch. XIII/XV), and as one of the stock speech topics of the tram-opening rally. Established renderings: English 'subbotnik' is in the OED and standard in Soviet-history writing; Chinese uses 星期六义务劳动 (full form 共产主义星期六义务劳动, as in the Chinese Lenin); Japanese uses スボートニク, glossed 土曜労働 or 勤労奉仕.

уездный город N.finding: «Город N» (also «уездный город N», «губернский город N», «город NN») is a stock fictional toponym of Russian literature for a remote, provincial, backwater town; it runs from Gogol (Dead Souls, The Inspector General) through Turgenev, Dostoevsky and Chekhov to Ilf and Petrov, and Russian Wikipedia has a dedicated article on the convention. The 'N' is a placeholder, never an initial to be expanded, and the phrase carries irony: stagnation, petty manners, provincial self-importance. «Уездный» marks the pre-revolutionary uezd (the county-level subdivision of a guberniya, formally abolished in 1923–29), so in a 1927 novel the label is itself a mild anachronism that sets the mock-classical tone; the town is only 'N' in Part One and is later revealed to be near Stargorod. Existing English translations do not agree: Richardson (1961) has 'the regional centre of N.', Anne O. Fisher (2011, Northwestern; 2012 NCBA award) has 'the provincial town of N.'. The current Chinese translation (白桦熊, 上海译文 2022) opens with 'N县城的理发馆和寿材铺是如此之多…', so 'N县城' is established in Chinese. The Japanese translation (江川卓訳『十二の椅子』筑摩書房 1969) exists but its exact wording for the town could not be verified online; Japanese reference works render уезд as 郡.

«Летопись войны 1914 года» / «Русский па.term: «Летопись войны 1914 года» / «Русский паломник» / «История раскола» / нижние чины / Перемышль
«Летопись войны 1914 года» / «Русский па.finding: All are real. In ch. 3 Father Fyodor's tin-bound trunk is lined with pictures cut from «Летопись войны 1914 года», the official illustrated war weekly edited by Maj.-Gen. D. N. Dubensky (Petrograd 1914–17, 132 issues), with the captions «Взятие Перемышля» and «Раздача теплых вещей нижним чинам на позициях»; inside lie a 1903 run of «Русский паломник», the mass-market Orthodox illustrated weekly (1885–1917, publisher P. P. Soikin, begun with John of Kronstadt's blessing), and «История раскола», i.e. Metropolitan Makary's standard seminary text on the 17th-century Old Believer schism (1855). «Нижние чины» is the imperial-army category for privates and NCOs as opposed to officers; Przemyśl (Russian Перемышль) is the Austro-Hungarian fortress that surrendered to Russia on 9/22 March 1915, the great patriotic headline of that spring. For a 1928 reader the set is a deadpan inventory of a provincial priest's dead pre-revolutionary world: loyalist war propaganda, pious reading, and seminary theology, now the wrapping for a get-rich scheme. Richardson's 1961 English gives 'Chronicle of the 1914 War', 'The Capture of Peremyshl', 'Distribution of Comforts to Other Ranks', 'Russian Pilgrim', 'History of the Schism'; Chinese and Japanese book translations are not online, but zh/ja Wikipedia fix the place name as 普热梅希尔 / プシェムィシル and the schism as 教会分裂 / 教会分裂 (古儀式派).

концессионеры.finding: A концессия in 1920s Soviet usage was a specific legal institution of NEP: under Lenin's decree of 23 Nov 1920 the state leased mines, oil fields, forests and factories to foreign capitalists (Harriman's manganese, Lena Goldfields, Japanese Sakhalin oil), supervised from 1923 by Glavkontsesskom; there were at most 103 active concessions (1926) and they were wound up after Dec 1930. In chapter VI Bender, negotiating his share, calls himself 'непосредственный участник концессии и технический руководитель дела', and the narrator immediately adopts the word ('своему новому компаньону и непосредственному участнику концессии'); thereafter 'концессионеры' is the narrator's fixed mock-official label for the pair, and Ilf and Petrov reuse it in The Golden Calf. For a 1928 reader the joke was that two shabby private treasure-hunters styled themselves after the foreign firms the newspapers wrote about with suspicion; the word was pompous, faintly disreputable and unmistakably NEP. Richardson's English (1961, lib.ru) uses 'concession' / 'the concessionaires' throughout and this has become the standard English label. Egawa Taku's Japanese translation (1969) makes the pair form a 共同利権会社, so 利権 is the established Japanese key; Japanese historiography uses both 利権 and コンセッション for Soviet NEP concessions (北樺太石油コンセッション). Zhang Peiwen's Chinese translation renders Bender's line with 合同 and 合伙人, dropping the institution; Chinese Soviet-history writing calls NEP concessions 租让制 / 租让企业, whereas 特许经营 today means commercial franchising.

«Всеобщая Электрическая Компания».finding: In ch. X Polesov complains that the Stargorod tram has 'четыре мотора «Всеобщей Электрической Компании»' that will just about run, while 'остальные моторы — харьковская работа'. «Всеобщая электрическая компания» is the standard Soviet-era Russian calque of the American General Electric Co.: Lenin's Imperialism (ch. V) uses 'Всеобщая электрич. Ко' for the US trust and 'Всеобщее общество электричества' for its German rival, and AEG's own Russian subsidiary (1901–1918) was named «Всеобщая компания электричества» (ВКЭ), not «электрическая компания». So the phrase denotes GE, and John Richardson's 1961 English translation already renders it 'four General Electric engines'. For a 1928 reader the contrast is imported American quality versus shoddy domestic 'Kharkov work' — with the extra irony, invisible today, that the Kharkov electrical works (later ХЭМЗ) was the former ВКЭ/AEG plant evacuated from Riga in 1915. Fixed corporate names: zh 通用电气公司, ja ゼネラル・エレクトリック (both Wikipedia titles). I could not access the published Chinese (张佩文, 2004) or Japanese (江川卓, 1969) translations of the passage.

дворник.finding: A dvornik was the live-in yard-keeper of a town apartment house: he swept the yard and pavement, locked and unlocked the street gate at night (tenants tipped him a grivennik to be let in — the 'night earnings' the No. 5 dvornik loses when Polesov removes the gates), and, since a decree following the 1866 attempt on Alexander II, served as an unpaid lowest rung of the police: he wore a numbered brass badge, carried a police whistle, checked residence papers, reported suspicious tenants, stood night watch and acted as witness at searches (rules codified 1896). The Kommersant history notes that in 1922 Moscow dvorniks received almost identical orders — report violations, assist the militia, night patrols, whistle and badge — so in 1928 a Russian reader still saw in him a petty, respected-and-feared authority figure, not a mere cleaner; only in the 1960s did he become 'a man with a broom'. Register in the novel is neutral-descriptive, mined for irony (Klavdia Ivanovna dreams of 'dvorniks playing harps'). In chapter X the dvornik of No. 5 does not literally chase Polesov: he comes to demand the gates, begs 'Christ God', utters vague threats, kicks the padlock, tears down Polesov's signboard and raises a public scandal until a militiaman drags him (the dvornik) to the district station — the joke being that the house's own mini-policeman ends up arrested. Existing renderings: Richardson's 1961 English uses 'caretaker' for Tikhon and 'yard-keeper' for exactly this No. 5 dvornik; Wiktionary lists yard-keeper/doorkeeper/caretaker/porter; standard Ru-Zh dictionaries give 看院子的/看院人; Japanese dictionaries give 庭番/管理人/用務員, with 庭番 the conventional choice in Russian-literature translations. I could not verify the Chinese (徐昌翰, 张佩文, 白桦熊) or Japanese (江川卓 1969) editions' wording online.

дворник.note_for_reader: A dvornik (yard-keeper) was the house's live-in sweeper and gate-locker who, since tsarist times and still under the 1920s militia, wore a badge, carried a police whistle and kept watch over the tenants — a lowly but real authority.
дворник.rationale: All three keep the denotation (courtyard + keeper/watcher: 'keeper', 看, 番) and the plain neutral register, and match the established renderings in existing translations and dictionaries; what is given up is the specific tsarist/NEP police-auxiliary connotation, which no target word carries and which the one-line note restores for the Polesov scene. Rejected: 'janitor'/管理人/用務員 (modern, purely custodial, kills the joke), 'dvornik' (opaque without a note anyway), 门房/門番 (too narrow: gatekeeper only).

Старкомхоз.finding: Старкомхоз is a fictional but perfectly formed 1920s Soviet stump-compound: Стар(городский) + ком(мунальное) хоз(яйство), i.e. the Stargorod Department of Communal Economy — the local-soviet body (real-life 'откомхоз', 'губкомхоз', 'коммунхоз', all attested in 1920s archives and in the Dictionary of Sovdep language) that ran housing, streets and pavements, parks, lighting, water, fire brigades and, here, the new tram. In the novel it appears in ch. XI, where the concessionaires learn that the housing division (жилотдел) was dissolved in 1921 and its files merged into the Starkomkhoz archive (archivist Korobeinikov), and in ch. XIII, where Gavrilin, 'заведующий Старкомхозом' just transferred from Samarkand, chairs the tram opening while Treukhov works in its 'отдел благоустройства'. To a 1928 reader it read as exact, slightly absurd bureaucratic shorthand — one of a chain of parodic acronyms (Старсобес, Старгико, Мельстрой) that the narrators use deadpan. John Richardson's 1961 English version renders it 'the Stargorod communal services' / 'Chairman of the Stargorod Communal Services' without the acronym; Anne O. Fisher's 2011 version could not be checked online, and no online text of the Chinese (徐昌翰/张佩文, 白桦熊) or Japanese (江川卓, 1969) translations was reachable, so the zh/ja renderings below are not verified against those editions. The prompt's reference to Durov, VKontakte and 2013 does not apply to this 1928 term.

великий комбинатор.finding: The narrator's mock-heroic standing epithet for Ostap Bender in both novels (chapter 5 of 'Двенадцать стульев' and a chapter of 'Золотой телёнок' bear the title). In 1920s Odessa/NEP speech 'комбинация' meant a clever, usually shady scheme and 'комбинатор' its author (Lechaim traces the formula to Sholem Aleichem's 'человек с комбинациями'); the pompous 'великий' is the authors' irony. It became a proverbial крылатое выражение: dictionaries define it as 'ловкий пройдоха, добивающийся успеха путём сложных операций, уловок, мошенничества', used colloquially with irony or disapproval, and in post-Soviet Russia (a Lenkom production 'Великий комбинатор' opened in the 2010s) it carries as much admiration for resourcefulness as reproach. Existing English translations split: Malamuth 'the great schemer', Richardson 1961 'the smooth operator' (also used in Fisher's presentation of The Little Golden Calf), Gurevich/Anderson 2009 'the grand strategist'; Chinese print translations use 伟大谋士 (张佩文, 人民文学 2004) and 大谋士 (徐昌翰, 江苏凤凰文艺 2022). The Japanese rendering in 江川卓's translation (筑摩書房 1961/1969) could not be verified online; Japanese coverage only paraphrases him as 稀代の詐欺師/ペテン師. The prompt's mention of Durov/VKontakte does not apply to this term.

Given up: the Odessa/Yiddish colouring of 'комбинация' and the outright con-man connotation of 'smooth operator', which today also evokes the Sade song.

The text introduces him as Александр Яковлевич; his wife Александра Яковлевна calls him Альхен and he calls her Сашхен — private pet-forms of Alexander/Alexandra, so the nickname must stay a nickname. The Chinese 张佩文 translation (人民文学 名著名译) renders him 阿尔亨, wife 萨什亨, chapter title 文过饰非的小偷 (other Chinese editions: 知耻无悔的小偷, 温文尔雅的小偷). Лед тронулся, господа присяжные заседате.finding: Ostap Bender's signature exclamation, first uttered in the chapter «Бриллиантовый дым» (ch. VI in the canonical text): while Vorobyaninov tells the story of the jewels, Ostap keeps jumping up and shouting it 'to the iron stove', then repeats it when they shake hands on the partnership. «Лёд тронулся» is the spring ice-break on a river (ледоход), used figuratively for 'things have finally started moving, the deadlock is over'; «господа присяжные заседатели» is the address a barrister used to the jury in the pre-revolutionary jury court, abolished in 1917, so in 1928 it is a mock-solemn anachronism, Ostap parodying courtroom oratory to give his swindle comic gravitas (it pairs with his other courtroom tag «Заседание продолжается»). The line became a proverb: Russian media still headline stalled projects that finally move with «Лёд тронулся». English coverage is split: the 1961 Richardson translation has 'Things are moving, gentlemen of the jury', Fisher's 2011 Northwestern translation is reported as 'The ice has started breaking up, gentlemen of the jury!', while Wikipedia and Russia Beyond use 'The ice has broken, (ladies and) gentlemen of the jury!'. Published Chinese (张佩文 2004; 白桦熊 2022, whose paratext popularises the sister tag 庭审继续进行) and Japanese (江川卓 1966/1969) renderings of this line could not be retrieved online. The prompt's reference to Durov/VKontakte coverage is unrelated to this term and was not pursued.

извозчик.finding: An извозчик was a licensed driver of a horse-drawn vehicle for hire (a droshky or пролётка), the pre-automobile urban taxi; Russian Wikipedia defines it as 'кучер гужевой повозки любого типа, предоставляющий услуги частного извоза' and distinguishes the cheap seasonal 'ванька', the stand-based 'биржевой' and the fast, expensive 'лихач'. In 1927 Moscow horse cabs still dominated: about 5,000 извозчики against roughly 120 state and 150 private motor taxis, and only by the mid-1930s (385 licences in 1934, 58 in 1939) were they displaced. In the novel the word is neutral everyday usage: the Moscow friends 'посадили парочку на извозчика' (ch. XX), 'Извозчик издал губами поцелуйный звук' to his horse (ch. XVI), and the drunken all-night ride ends with Ippolit Matveyevich befriending a лихач who exclaims 'Веселый барин!' — the pre-revolutionary 'барин' from a cabman is itself part of the joke. Existing translations: English Chekhov/Ilf-Petrov practice is 'cabman/cabby/cab driver' (no established 'horse-cab driver'); Chinese Russian-literature translations (Chekhov's 苦恼) use 马车夫/车夫; Japanese uses 辻馬車 for the hired carriage and 御者 for its driver. Гусище.finding: Gusishche is a fictional outlying district (окраина) of the fictional Stargorod, not a separate town. In Chapter XI ('Алфавит «Зеркало жизни»') Ostap crosses the whole city to reach it: 'Коробейников жил на Гусище — окраине Старгорода. Там жили преимущественно железнодорожники' — a railway embankment runs above the houses, shunting locomotives light the roofs, and the archivist-pawnbroker Korobeinikov is known there as Варфоломеич. In Chapter XIII ('Дышите глубже: вы взволнованы!') it is where depot workers and rope-makers dug holes at a 1920 subbotnik and where the new tram depot stands, so all Stargorod marches to Gusishche on May Day and the first trams glide 'цугом по Гусищу' under the railway bridge. So it is a working-class railwaymen's edge-of-town quarter; the gloss 'seen from the train' is loose, the district is seen from the street with trains passing above it. The name is a comic-rustic Russian toponym built like Городище/Слободище: гусь 'goose' plus the augmentative place-suffix -ище, so a 1928 reader heard something like 'Big Goose Place'. John Richardson's standard English translation (1961) writes 'Gusishe'; Anne O. Fisher's 2011 Northwestern translation exists but I could not verify its spelling online, and no Chinese or Japanese rendering could be found online (the 张佩文 and 江川卓 translations are not searchable).
