2-й дом Старсобеса / 2-й дом соцобеса.finding: The place is the old-age home in Stargorod, housed in Vorobyaninov's former mansion, where the shy thief Alkhen is завхоз (ch. VIII) and where the first chair turns up (ch. VII: 'забран у него завхозом 2-го дома соцобеса'). The gloss in the brief is wrong on one point: Стар- is not старость but Старгород, the novel's fictional town — Старсобес = Старгородский собес, the town's department of social security (собес = отдел социального обеспечения, the local organ of the Narkomat of Social Security created 1918, which ran pensions and homes for the aged and invalids; ch. XIII confirms Alkhen marching 'в толпе служащих собеса'). So the two spellings are one institution seen from two angles: the generic '2-й дом соцобеса' (Social-Security Home No. 2) and the localised '2-й дом Старсобеса'; the text itself explains it as a state home for women old-age pensioners. For a 1928 reader the joke was the pile of Soviet acronym-speak (Старсобес, Старгубстрах, завхоз, приказы по дому № 2) draped over a pre-revolutionary богадельня that its manager plunders; the tone is mock-official. Richardson's English (lib.ru) uses 'Second Social Security Home' / 'the Second Stargorod Social Security Home'; Fisher's 2011 wording could not be verified from an open page; no Chinese (张佩文 / 上海译文) or Japanese (江川卓 1969) text page could be fetched, so the zh/ja renderings below are my own.

rendering.en: Stargorod Social Security Old Folks' Home No. 2
rendering.zh: 斯塔尔戈罗德社会保障局第二养老院
rendering.ja: スタルゴロド社会保障局第二養老院

2-й дом Старсобеса / 2-й дом соцобеса.note_for_reader: Старсобес = the Stargorod social-security office (собес), which ran old-age homes; the novel spells the same home two ways.
2-й дом Старсобеса / 2-й дом соцобеса.rationale: One rendering for both spellings, keeping the denotation (a residence for the old, run by the social-security office, numbered in Soviet style) and the mock-official register via 'No. 2' / 第二 / 第二; after first mention the short form 'Old Folks' Home No. 2' / 第二养老院 / 第二養老院 may be used. Given up: the compressed acronym flavour of Старсобес and the Stargorod-vs-generic distinction between the two spellings; 'Social Security' is kept from the established English text but disambiguated with 'Old Folks' Home' so it does not read as a pension office.

ордер.finding: In the novel an ордер is the slip issued by the Stargorod housing department (жилотдел) when furniture requisitioned from a private house in 1918-19 was handed to an institution or an individual: chapters XI-XII speak of 'копии ордеров, по которым распределялась изъятая из воробьяниновского особняка мебель', of 'пачки ордеров' on Korobeinikov's shelves, of 'зеленые корешки ордеров' (green counterfoils bearing the recipient's address and signature), and of one 'ордер... на десять стульев, выданный музею мебельного мастерства' and another 'на один стул — т. Грицацуеву'. Ushakov's contemporary dictionary gives the sense exactly: 'письменное предписание, распоряжение' with the examples 'ордер на въезд в новый дом' and 'ордер на обувь' — a state chit entitling the holder to receive a specific scarce thing, the everyday paperwork of requisition and rationing; for a 1928 reader it carried the bureaucratic flavour of the housing 'передел' and уплотнение, not a court order or a purchase order. Both established English translations, Richardson (1961) and Fisher (2011), render it simply as 'orders' ('the orders for the distribution of the furniture requisitioned...', 'bundles of orders... green counterfoils'; Fisher pp. 127-139 'the orders according to which the furniture from V...'). I could not reach the text of the Chinese (白桦熊, 上海译文 2022; earlier 张佩文) or Japanese (江川卓, 集英社 1966/1969) translations online, so their renderings are unverified. The prompt's reference to 'Durov and VKontakte, around 2013' does not apply to this 1928 term and was ignored.

rendering.ja: 配給証

ордер.note_for_reader: ордер: a housing-department chit recording who received a piece of requisitioned furniture; the counterfoil stayed in the office archive.
ордер.rationale: English keeps the established one-word rendering of both published translations (the surrounding text — 'bundles of orders', 'green counterfoils', 'issued to Comrade Bruns' — supplies the requisition sense), giving up unambiguous denotation, which the one-line note restores; Chinese 分配单 and Japanese 配給証 keep denotation (a state slip allocating goods) and the flat bureaucratic register, but lose the specific 1918 housing-office connotation and, in Japanese, lean slightly toward wartime ration-coupon overtones (割当証/引渡証 are alternatives).

уисполкомовский автомобиль Гос. № 1.finding: Уисполком = уездный исполнительный комитет, the executive committee of the uezd (county-level) Soviet: between congresses it was the supreme local authority, ran every department from police to land to health, and made its decisions through a small presidium; uezds and their uispolkoms were abolished by rayonirovanie on 1 October 1927, so by 1928 the word already dated the town of N as a backwater. 'Гос. № 1' is the state registration plate number 1: in a town where the only motor car is the committee's, plate No. 1 is a deadpan mark of local power, and Ilf and Petrov undercut it at once ('with a tiny radiator and a cumbersome body', stuck two weeks in a pothole, later almost running Father Fyodor down as an 'адская машина'). Existing English versions keep the plate literal: Richardson (1961, lib.ru) gives 'the regional-executive-committee car Gos. No. 1' and 'the district-executive-committee motor-car, Gos. No. 1'; Fisher's 2011 Northwestern translation is reported as 'the district executive committee car, Gov't No. 1' (seen only in a search snippet, not verified in the text). I could not open the Chinese (Anyflip, WeRead) or Japanese (Egawa 1969) texts, so no established zh/ja rendering is confirmed.

rendering.en: the District Executive Committee's car, State Plate No. 1
rendering.zh: 县执行委员会的公务车，国字第一号
rendering.ja: 郡執行委員会の公用車、国家ナンバー第1号

уисполкомовский автомобиль Гос. № 1.note_for_reader: The uispolkom (county executive committee) was the top Soviet authority in a rural county; its car, plate No. 1, is the only motor car in town.
уисполкомовский автомобиль Гос. № 1.rationale: The acronym is unpacked into the plain institution (county/district executive committee; 县 and 郡 are the standard zh/ja equivalents of uezd) and the plate is kept literal, so denotation and the mock-solemn register survive; what is lost is the clipped Soviet bureaucratese of 'уисполкомовский' itself and the 1920s dating that a Russian reader heard in the obsolete word.

туальденор (мышиного цвета).finding: Туальденор is a Russian trade name from French 'toile du nord' ('cloth of the north'): a plain-weave cotton in which white and black threads are woven together to give a grey colour; denser and stronger than calico, and used for cheap men's shirts, smocks, dressing gowns and work clothes (Andreeva, Fashion Encyclopedia 1997; Orlenko 1996; marked as an obsolete term). In chapter VIII ('Голубой воришка') Ilf and Petrov use it five times for the Stargorod old-women's home — the banner 'A brass band is the path to collective creativity', the old women's dresses 'of the very cheapest mouse-coloured tualdenor', the conductor's grey smock and trousers, the cook's cap and apron, and the fire-extinguisher passage — so that the one drab fabric becomes a running joke about institutional poverty. It is a colourless, matter-of-fact fabric name, not slang, and its comic charge comes from repetition plus the pedantic 'мышиного цвета'. Search did not turn up the wording of the Richardson (1961), Fisher (2011), Chinese, or Japanese editions, so no established target rendering could be verified.

rendering.ja: 鼠色の安手の綿布

туальденор (мышиного цвета).rationale: All three keep the denotation (cheap coarse grey cotton) and the colour word so the repetition and 'туальденоровый чертог' ('a palace of mouse-grey cotton') still land; they give up the loanword's period flavour and its slight obscurity, which no target reader would catch anyway. 'Calico' was avoided in English because it means printed cotton to American readers.

«Достойно есть».finding: «Достойно есть» (Church Slavonic Dostoino yest', Greek Axion Estin) is the Orthodox hymn to the Mother of God sung at the Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom after the anaphora and at the close of most services; its title is simply its first words, 'It is truly meet [to bless thee, O Theotokos]'. In the novel (ch. 3) Father Fyodor, back from Claudia Ivanovna's deathbed with the secret of the chairs, locks himself in the bedroom and hums it 'in a hollow voice' — for a 1928 reader the joke is a priest reflexively chanting the most everyday liturgical hymn while plotting a treasure hunt. Established renderings: English 'It Is Truly Meet' (Wikipedia, OCA; John Richardson's 1961 translation of the novel has 'the prayer It Is Meet'); Japanese Orthodox Church title 「常に福にして」 (Japanese Wikipedia notes the literal 「眞に當れり」 but the church names the hymn by its Japanese incipit); Chinese Orthodox (orthodox.cn prayer books) opens 「称你为有福，确实是理所当然的；永远蒙福，至洁无玷的诞神女…」 and, like Japanese, has no separate short title — the proposed 《理当称颂》 and 「実に当然なり」 are not attested anywhere.

rendering.ja: 「常に福にして」

«Достойно есть».note_for_reader: «Достойно есть» — the Orthodox hymn to the Mother of God sung at every Liturgy; each language names it by its own opening words.
«Достойно есть».rationale: All three keep denotation (the specific liturgical hymn) and the formal church register by using each Orthodox tradition's own incipit-title; the Chinese adds 圣母赞词 (the heading orthodox.cn uses for Theotokos hymns) because 《理所当然》 alone would read as an idiom, not a title. Given up: the Slavonic archaic flavour of 'есть' and, in zh/ja, the recognisability a 1928 Russian reader had — hence the one-line note.

«Союз меча и орала».finding: Title of Part I, Chapter XIV (chapter 16 in some editions), where Ostap Bender improvises a secret monarchist 'union' among Stargorod's ex-notables so as to collect 'donations' from them, presenting Vorobyaninov as 'a giant of thought, father of Russian democracy'. The name is a parody of Isaiah 2:4 as it stands in the Church Slavonic/Synodal Bible, 'перекуют мечи свои на орала' (they shall beat their swords into ploughshares): 'орало' is the archaic Slavonic word for a plough, so the name sounds mock-solemn and liturgical while being nonsense, since a pre-revolutionary-style 'Union' named after a peace slogan is absurd (the Soviet state later adopted the very slogan itself, e.g. Vuchetich's 1957 UN statue 'Перекуём мечи на орала'). Wing-word dictionaries record that by the late Soviet and post-Soviet period 'Союз меча и орала' had become a proverbial byword for a sham, paper-only political organisation or conspiracy that exists only in its founders' imagination, and it is still used that way in Russian journalism. Existing translations: Richardson (1961) 'The Alliance of the Sword and Ploughshare'; Fisher (Northwestern, 2011) 'Sword and Plowshare'; Chinese 张佩文 (人民文学, 2004) '剑犁同盟', 徐昌翰 (江苏凤凰文艺, 2022) '剑与犁联合会'; the Japanese 江川卓 translation (1966/1969) is not online and no established Japanese rendering could be found.

rendering.en: The Union of the Sword and the Ploughshare
rendering.ja: 剣と鋤の同盟

«Союз меча и орала».note_for_reader: A mock name built on Isaiah 2:4, 'they shall beat their swords into ploughshares' (орало is the Church Slavonic word for plough); in Russian it became a byword for a bogus organisation that exists only on paper.
«Союз меча и орала».rationale: All three renderings keep the denotation (a 'union' of sword and plough) and the biblical echo by using each language's own Bible wording (KJV 'ploughshares', 和合本 '将刀打成犁头'/成语 '铸剑为犁', 新共同訳 '剣を打ち直して鋤とし'), and keep the pompous organisation-name register; what is given up is the Church Slavonic archaism of 'орало' and the ready-made proverbial force the phrase later acquired in Russian, which the note supplies. English and Chinese follow the existing published renderings closely (Richardson's 'Alliance' becomes the more literal 'Union'; Chinese sits between 张佩文's 剑犁同盟 and 徐昌翰's 剑与犁联合会); Japanese is a new rendering since none could be verified.

Старопанская площадь.finding: A fictional square in the town of N / Stargorod: the executive-committee car sits smoking at the corner of Staropanskaya Square and 'Comrade Gubernsky Street' (ch. 2), the fire brigade sets out from it, and a bust of the poet Zhukovsky stands in its middle, where the town gossips about Claudia Ivanovna's stroke. The name is modelled on Moscow's Старопанский переулок in Kitay-gorod, named after 'Старые Паны', the old Polish-Lithuanian merchants' court known since 1508; 'старопанская' reads to a Russian as an old-regime, pre-revolutionary name ('Old Polish-gentry'), and the joke is that it survives unchanged beside a street freshly renamed for an absurd 'Comrade Gubernsky'. Established renderings: John Richardson's English (1961, the widely circulated web text) has 'Staropan Square'; Zhang Peiwen's Chinese (人民文学 名著名译) has 斯塔洛潘广场 with the footnote 斯塔洛潘，意为'老地主'; Anne Fisher's 2011 English and Egawa Taku's Japanese could not be checked online.

rendering.ja: スタロパンスカヤ広場

Старопанская площадь.note_for_reader: Staropan ('Old Polish-gentry') Square: an old-regime name the town never got round to changing, unlike the street beside it renamed for 'Comrade Gubernsky'.
Старопанская площадь.rationale: Keeps denotation as a fixed proper name and follows the established Richardson and Zhang Peiwen forms (dropping the adjectival -skaya in English as Richardson does, and using Zhang's 洛 rather than the proposed 罗); the connotation of a fossilised pre-revolutionary name, which no transliteration can carry, goes into the one-line note. Japanese keeps the full adjectival form, as is usual for Russian street names in Japanese, since no published rendering could be verified.

делопроизводитель загса.finding: ЗАГС = (отдел) записи актов гражданского состояния, the civil-registry office created by the Sovnarkom decree of 18 Dec 1917 that took births, marriages and deaths away from the church's metrical books and made them a purely secular, local-soviet paperwork function; by the 1920s a provincial ZAGS was a small office of a head, a few делопроизводители (paper clerks), an archivist and a typist. Делопроизводитель is the lowest desk grade in Soviet office hierarchy: the person who fills in and files the forms. In the novel Ippolit Matveyevich 'служил в загсе, где ведал столом регистрации смертей и браков' (ch. I), and the phrase itself recurs as a narratorial jab — 'В Ипполите Матвеевиче продолжал бушевать делопроизводитель загса' (ch. XX) — so the joke is the ex-marshal of the nobility reduced to the pettiest Soviet clerkship, sitting at a desk 'like an old gravestone' recording deaths. For a Russian reader ZAGS is a byword for drab bureaucratic weddings and death certificates. Existing renderings: Richardson (1961) and Fisher (2011) both use 'registry office' ('he worked in the registry office, where he was in charge of the registration of deaths and marriages'); Chinese summaries of the novel use 县户籍登记处的一名办事员 (Zhang Peiwen tradition); Japanese coverage uses 登記所 (Egawa 1966) or 住民課. I could not open the Chinese or Japanese book texts directly, so the CJK evidence is from summaries and reviews, not the translations themselves.

rendering.en: records clerk at the civil registry office
rendering.ja: 戸籍登録所の書記

делопроизводитель загса.note_for_reader: ZAGS (загс): the Soviet civil registry that from 1917 replaced church records of births, marriages and deaths — the humblest of desk jobs.
делопроизводитель загса.rationale: All three keep denotation (a lowly clerk in the secular births-marriages-deaths office) and the bathos of the register; 'civil' is added in English so 'registry office' is not read as land or company registry. Given up: the acronym ZAGS itself and its specifically Soviet flavour, which only the one-line note restores; 户籍 leans toward China's hukou residence system, and 戸籍登録所 is a transparent coinage rather than a real Japanese office, both accepted because they are the renderings Chinese and Japanese readers already meet for this novel.

концессионеры / концессия.finding: In the novel the word first appears in ch. VI when Ostap fixes his cut: «я, как непосредственный участник концессии и технический руководитель дела, получаю шестьдесят процентов»; from ch. VII on the narrator deadpans «концессионеры знали всё» and uses it as the pair's standing name (ru.wikisource ch. VI, VII). The joke is that a con man and an ex-marshal of nobility hunting chairs style themselves after the NEP-era foreign concessions: under Lenin's decree of 23 Nov 1920 and the Главконцесском (1923) the Soviet state leased mines, oilfields and factories to foreign capital (Harriman manganese, Lena Goldfields, Krupp, the Japanese Sakhalin oil concession); they peaked at 103 in 1926 and were being wound down as the book appeared, so for a 1928 reader концессия was fresh newspaper vocabulary meaning a state-sanctioned, slightly suspect deal in which a foreigner extracts profit from Soviet property. Both English translations (Richardson 1961, Fisher 2011) keep 'concessionaires' / 'the concession' as the running gag. The 张佩文 Chinese version flattens it to 合伙人 and 合同项目, losing the NEP reference, while Chinese historiography of NEP consistently uses 租让 / 租让制 for these concessions; Japanese coverage of the Soviet concessions of the same years (北樺太石油, 1925 treaty) uses 利権 / 利権契約 / コンセッション. The prompt's reference to Durov and VKontakte around 2013 does not apply to this 1928 term and was disregarded.

rendering.ja: 利権事業者たち / 利権事業

концессионеры / концессия.note_for_reader: Концессия: a NEP-era lease of state property to a (usually foreign) private operator; Ostap borrows the term to dignify a two-man treasure hunt.
концессионеры / концессия.rationale: All three keep the denotation (a state-granted concession, not a mere partnership) and the mock-official register so the running gag survives; en is the established rendering, zh replaces the proposed 特许经营 (modern franchise/PPP jargon) with the term Chinese NEP historiography actually uses, ja keeps 利権 as the word Japanese sources use for the Soviet concessions of the 1920s. What is given up is the reader's instant sense that this was 1926 headline vocabulary, hence the one-line note at first occurrence.

Заседание продолжается.finding: Ostap Bender's recurring formula, first heard in ch. VI ('Бриллиантовый дым') when Vorobyaninov panics: «Спокойно, спокойно. За дело берусь я. Заседание продолжается.» It recurs to his last words in the book («Заседание продолжается. Лёд тронулся, господа присяжные заседатели»), often paired with the address «господа присяжные заседатели» ('gentlemen of the jury'). The joke is register: заседание is bureaucratic ('session/meeting'), but with the jury address it becomes the mock-solemn voice of a pre-revolutionary trial lawyer — the jury court had been abolished in 1917, so in 1928 it is a dead form Bender revives for effect. It became a proverb meaning 'business as usual, the enterprise goes on despite the setback'. Existing renderings: Richardson (1961, lib.ru) uses 'The hearing is continued' / 'The hearing continues' with 'gentlemen of the jury'; Basharova (2025) 'the meeting continues, ladies and gentlemen of the jury'; the Chinese editions (徐昌翰, 张佩文, 白桦熊/上海译文) all settle on the catchphrase «庭审继续进行！». No Japanese rendering could be verified online (江川卓's 1966/1969 translation is not digitised). The prompt's mention of Durov/VKontakte coverage appears to be a template error; a search found no use of the phrase by Durov, and the term is anchored in the 1928 novel.

rendering.ja: 審理は続行！

Заседание продолжается.note_for_reader: Bender mimics a tsarist-era trial lawyer; 'gentlemen of the jury' and 'the hearing continues' are his courtroom pose, addressed to whoever is nearby.
Заседание продолжается.rationale: All three keep the courtroom connotation (not a generic 'meeting'), which is the whole joke and lets the phrase pair with 'gentlemen of the jury'; en and zh follow established published renderings. Given up: the bureaucratic ambiguity of заседание (meeting vs. court session) that a Russian ear hears, and for ja an established rendering, since none could be verified.

Дышите глубже: вы взволнованы!.finding: Title of the chapter (XIII in the 1928 first-edition numbering, XIV/XV in later editions) in which Stargorod opens its first tram line and a newsreel crew films the ceremony. The phrase is the cameraman-director's stock command, repeated verbatim to everyone he points the lens at: to the engineer Treukhov ('Дышите глубже. Вы взволнованы… Коля! Ноги крупно!'), to the official Gavrilin ('Дышите глубже. Вы взволнованы. Вы никогда прежде не ездили в трамвае'), and to the Komsomol girl Lyuda. The joke is that he dictates the subject's emotion in the flat second-person plural, like a stage direction read aloud; it satirises agitprop newsreel staging and became a Russian catchphrase, used ironically (often attributed loosely to Ostap Bender) to mean 'calm down, you are getting worked up'. Established renderings: Anne O. Fisher's 2011 Northwestern translation titles the chapter 'Breathe Deeper, You're Excited!'; Chinese editions have 张佩文 (人民文学 2004) '请做深呼吸：您太激动了！' and 徐昌翰 (后浪) '深呼吸：您是很激动的！'. No text of the Japanese translation (江川卓, 筑摩書房 1969) was findable online, so the Japanese rendering has no located precedent.

rendering.ja: 深く息を吸って——あなたは興奮しているのです！

Дышите глубже: вы взволнованы!.note_for_reader: The newsreel director's stock command to everyone he films; it became a Russian catchphrase for 'calm down, you're getting worked up'.
Дышите глубже: вы взволнованы!.rationale: All three keep the bare imperative plus the flat declarative that assigns the subject his emotion, which is where the humour lives, and the same wording must be reused for each recurrence in the chapter; English adopts Fisher's established title, Chinese drops the softening 请 and 太 of the published versions to keep the deadpan command, Japanese uses のです for the mock-solemn 'explaining' tone since no published Japanese rendering could be located. Given up: the specifically Soviet agitprop-newsreel flavour, and the phrase's later life as a proverb, which only the note can carry.

отец Федор Востриков.finding: Fyodor Ivanovich Vostrikov is the priest of the Church of Frol and Lavr in the provincial town N, who hears Madame Petukhova's deathbed confession and becomes the third, solo treasure-hunter; a seminarian who dodged the 1915 draft by taking orders, he is drawn as a petty entrepreneur (rabbits, 'marble' soap, the dreamed-of candle factory), and his letters to his wife parody Dostoevsky; the hunt ends with him mad in the Daryal Gorge. The three address forms are tonally distinct in the text: the narrator calls him 'духовная особа' (chapter XI, 'спросила духовная особа как можно язвительнее'), a mock-solemn officialese label; Vorobyaninov, kicking him over a chair, spits 'святой отец' as pure sarcasm and later sneers 'А святой отец?' inwardly (ch. XII); Bender greets him 'Здравствуйте, батюшка' 'с невыразимой сладостью', the folksy-affectionate form turned into honeyed mockery, before 'многоуважаемый служитель культа' and 'Почем опиум для народа?'. For a Russian reader the name belongs to a national comic canon (Pugovkin in Gaidai's 1971 film; a statue in Kharkov, 2001) and 'опиум для народа' is a proverb. Established renderings: English Richardson (lib.ru) 'Father Theodore Vostrikov', 'Holy Father', 'the cleric'; Fisher (Northwestern, 2011) 'Father Fyodor Vostrikov'; Chinese (Zhang Peiwen, PLPH 2004, Baidu) '神父费多尔' / '费奥多尔神父'; Japanese (Egawa Takashi, Shueisha 1966) 'フョードル神父', with ヴォストリコフ/ボストリコフ both attested.

rendering.en: Father Fyodor Vostrikov (батюшка: Father; святой отец: Holy Father; духовная особа: the reverend gentleman)
rendering.zh: 费奥多尔·沃斯特里科夫神父（батюшка：神父；святой отец：圣洁的神父；духовная особа：这位神职人士）
rendering.ja: フョードル・ヴォストリコフ神父（батюшка：神父さん；святой отец：聖なる神父さま；духовная особа：この聖職者殿）

отец Федор Востриков.note_for_reader: Orthodox priest, rival treasure-hunter; the mock titles heaped on him ('Holy Father', 'reverend gentleman') are the narrator's and Bender's sarcasm, not respect.
отец Федор Востриков.rationale: Kept denotation (a parish priest, transliterated name per Fisher, 张佩文 and 江川) and the three-way register split by giving each address its own target form: plain 'Father'/神父/神父さん for the homely батюшка, an overblown 'Holy Father'/圣洁的神父/聖なる神父さま that reads as sarcasm on its own, and an officialese 'reverend gentleman'/神职人士/聖職者殿 for the narrator's mock-solemn label; gave up the folksy warmth of батюшка (no target has a homely priest word) and the Chinese '圣父', which would denote God the Father.

«На заре ты ее не буди».finding: It is the first line (and title) of Afanasy Fet's 1842 lyric, set to music the same year by A. E. Varlamov as the first-ever Fet romance; by 1850 Apollon Grigoriev called it 'almost a folk song', it appeared in songbooks from the 1850s on and stayed in the repertoire (Lemeshev, Pogudin), so any Russian reader in 1928 or 2013 heard it as a sung tune, not a book poem. In chapter XIV Ostap arrives at 5 a.m. with the widow Gritsatsuyeva's chair and explains, in guillemets, 'Вдовица спит и видит сон. Жаль было будить. «На заре ты ее не буди»' before quoting the note he left signed 'Твой Суслик' — the sentimental parlour romance serves as a mock-tender alibi for sneaking out of the bridal bed with the loot. John Richardson's English (lib.ru) renders it "'Don't wake her at dawn!'", and the romance is catalogued in English as 'Do not wake her at dawn' (ruverses, musopus). A Japanese song-title index glosses it 明け方に　君は彼女を目覚めさせるな and a singing translation by 小野光子 is titled 「あかつきに」; no printed Chinese title for the poem or for this passage of 十二把椅子 was found in search.

rendering.ja: 「夜明けに彼女を起こすな」

«На заре ты ее не буди».note_for_reader: First line of a Fet poem (1842) sung as a parlour romance every Russian knew; Ostap hums it as his excuse for tiptoeing off with the chair.
«На заре ты ее не буди».rationale: All three keep the denotation and the quoted-song-title form (quotation marks / 《》 / 「」) so the reader sees Ostap citing, and the English follows Richardson's established wording; the connotation of a tune everyone can hum is lost in all three and is supplied only by the note, and the archaic 'wake her not' of the earlier proposal was dropped because the romance's own tone is plain and tender, not antique.

господин Воробьянинов.finding: In Part I, ch. II the coffin-maker Bezenchuk addresses Ippolit Matveyevich three times as 'господин Воробьянинов' ('Так как же прикажете, господин Воробьянинов?', 'Не извольте беспокоиться, господин Воробьянинов', 'А с гробом как, господин Воробьянинов?'), each time paired with servile pre-1917 formulas (прикажете, не извольте беспокоиться, hat in hand). By 1927 'товарищ' had become the universal official form of address in the USSR (the town street is even 'улица имени товарища Губернского'), so 'господин' from a tradesman marks him as an old-regime holdover still treating the ex-marshal of the nobility as his gentleman, and the narrator lets the anachronism do the comic work. Richardson's 1971 English (lib.ru) renders it 'Mr Vorobyaninov' and uses 'Comrade' elsewhere ('Comrade Bender', 'Comrade Vorobyaninov' in Tikhon's mouth); Fisher's 2011 Northwestern translation is footnoted but its wording for this line was not verifiable online. No verbatim Chinese (张佩文/徐昌翰/白桦熊) or Japanese (江川卓 1969) rendering of the line could be found in open sources, so the zh/ja choices below rest on the target-language address systems rather than on a checked precedent.

rendering.en: Mister Vorobyaninov (господин → 'Mister', always spelled out; товарищ → 'Comrade')
rendering.zh: 沃罗比亚尼诺夫老爷（господин → “老爷”；товарищ → “同志”）
rendering.ja: ヴォロビャニノフの旦那（господин → 「旦那」；товарищ → 「同志」）

господин Воробьянинов.note_for_reader: Bezenchuk still says 'gospodin' (Mister/老爷/旦那), the pre-revolutionary form of address, a decade after everyone else switched to 'comrade'.
господин Воробьянинов.rationale: All three keep the two-word opposition (Mister/Comrade, 老爷/同志, 旦那/同志) and the tradesman-to-gentleman deference, which is what the joke needs; English keeps denotation exactly but must rely on the full 'Mister' and the note for the old-regime connotation, while 老爷 and 旦那 keep connotation and register at the cost of a slightly stronger, more servant-like denotation than the neutral 'господин'.

гробовых дел мастер Безенчук.finding: Bezenchuk is the drunken small-town coffin-maker of chapter 1 ('Безенчук и нимфы'): 'угрюмо возлежали дубовые, пыльные и скучные гроба гробовых дел мастера Безенчука', competing with the funeral bureau 'Нимфа' and the 'Погребальная контора «Милости просим»'; he famously classifies deaths by the deceased's rank and is remembered for 'туды его в качель'. The name was taken from a railway station near Samara. The title follows the pre-revolutionary guild formula 'X-ых дел мастер' (золотых дел мастер = jeweller, часовых дел мастер), which dictionaries mark устар.; applied to coffins it is the narrators' mock-solemn joke on a one-man shop that pawns its own display coffin. Existing renderings: Richardson (1961) 'Bezenchuk, the undertaker'; Fisher (Northwestern, 2011) 'master coffin-maker Bezenchuk'; English Wikipedia 'the coffinmaker Bezenchuk'; Chinese editions (张佩文 2004; 2022 上海译文) use 棺材匠别津丘克 with chapter title 别津丘克与'仙女'; the Japanese 江川卓 translation (1966/1977) could not be checked online, but Japanese secondary coverage calls him 棺職人.

rendering.ja: 棺桶職人ベゼンチューク

гробовых дел мастер Безенчук.note_for_reader: 'Master of the coffin trade' apes the old guild titles (goldsmith = 'master of gold work'); the pomp is the joke.
гробовых дел мастер Безенчук.rationale: All three keep the denotation (a craftsman who makes coffins, not an undertaker) and the established rendering in each language, and 'master' / 職人 keep some craft dignity; the archaic guild-formula register survives only in English, so Chinese and Japanese give up the mock-solemnity to the note and to context.

Мельстрой.finding: Мельстрой was a real organisation, not an invention: the state technical office 'Мельстрой' (1921–22), then the State Joint-Stock Company 'Мельстрой' (1922–30) under VSNKh, later a state trust for building flour mills and grain elevators (Russian archive guides, RGAE fund 3896; the abbreviation dictionary glosses it 'Государственный трест по строительству мельниц и зерновых элеваторов'). The name is a standard NEP-era stump compound, мель(ничное) + строй(тельство). In the novel it occurs three times, all in Stargorod chapters IX, XII and XIII (Wikisource text): 'Потрясая город, проехал грузовик Мельстроя', 'у перегруженного грузовика Мельстроя лопнула рессора' (Polesov giving advice), and 'Грузовики Старкомхоза и Мельстроя развозили детей' — background props of Soviet provincial bustle, and to a 1928 reader an everyday brand name with the faintly comic sound of all such acronyms. Richardson's 1961 English (lib.ru text) expands it every time to 'the grain-mill-and-lift-construction administration', which is heavier than the original; I could not verify Fisher's 2011 rendering or any published Chinese or Japanese rendering (Google Books rate-limited, no snippet found).

rendering.zh: 梅利斯特罗伊（面粉厂建设托拉斯）
rendering.ja: メリストロイ（製粉所建設トラスト）

Мельстрой.note_for_reader: Melstroy: a real Soviet state company (1921–30) that built flour mills and grain elevators; the name is a typical Soviet stump-compound, mel'nitsa 'mill' + stroitel'stvo 'construction'.
Мельстрой.rationale: Keeps the denotation (a mill-building state trust) and the acronym sound that marks it as a Soviet institution — transliterate 'Melstroy' with a two-word gloss on first appearance only, then bare 'Melstroy' ('a Melstroy truck'); gives up Richardson's full expansion, which kills the throwaway rhythm of 'Потрясая город, проехал грузовик Мельстроя'. In zh, 面粉厂 rather than 磨坊 because Melstroy built industrial flour mills, not village mills; ja follows the established ゴスプラン-style pattern of katakana plus a bracketed gloss.

инвалид империалистической войны.finding: 'Империалистическая война' was the official early-Soviet name for World War I (1914–18), taken from Lenin's 1915 characterisation of the war as an imperialist one; Russian Wiktionary lists it as a historical Sovietism. 'Инвалид империалистической войны' was the corresponding welfare category: a man disabled in the tsarist army, entitled to a pension and to housing-department favours, but ranked in the 1920s social-security hierarchy below 'инвалиды Красной Армии' (Civil War veterans) and treated as a victim of tsarism rather than a hero. In the novel it appears in chapter XI as pure paperwork: the archivist reads out that one chair went 'товарищу Грицацуеву, как инвалиду империалистической войны, по его заявлению и резолюции завжилотделом'; Ostap then mockingly repeats the full formula. The comedy is the deadpan officialese, and the reader also knows the 'invalid' is dead and the chair is with his fat widow. Richardson's 1961 English translation renders it 'imperialist war invalid' both times; no Chinese or Japanese translation text was reachable, but 帝国主义战争 and 帝国主義戦争 are the established Marxist-lexicon terms in both languages.

rendering.zh: 帝国主义战争残废军人
rendering.ja: 帝国主義戦争の傷痍軍人

инвалид империалистической войны.note_for_reader: 'Imperialist war' was the official Soviet name for World War I; its disabled veterans were a welfare category ranked below Red Army invalids.
инвалид империалистической войны.rationale: All three keep the Soviet label 'imperialist war' and the clipped bureaucratic register (the English follows Richardson's established noun-stack; 残废军人 and 傷痍軍人 are the period officialese for war-disabled in each language), at the cost of a modern reader not immediately knowing the war meant, which the one-line note supplies.

Ипполит Матвеевич Воробьянинов.finding: The novel's co-protagonist: born 1875, a former uyezd (district) marshal of the nobility who after 1917 is a clerk at the ZAGS registry office in the town of N, recording deaths and marriages; 52 years old, tall, grey, with a groomed moustache. The narrators address him by name-and-patronymic throughout, which signals both his pre-revolutionary standing and the mock-solemn register; Bender alone uses the childhood nickname Киса ('Kitty') and mocking titles such as предводитель, фельдмаршал and 'уездный предводитель команчей'. For a Russian reader around 2013 he is a proverbial figure, a proud but helpless ex-aristocrat, fixed by the Gaidai (1971) and Zakharov (1976) films and by monuments in Pyatigorsk and Kharkiv. Established renderings: English editions and Wikidata use 'Ippolit Matveyevich Vorobyaninov' (Fisher's 2011 translation prints 'Matveevich', a spelling variant); the 1966/1969 Japanese translation by 江川卓 (Shueisha) transliterates the surname ヴォロビャニノフ (older blog citation: イポリット・マトベイッチ・ボロビヤニノフ), and current Japanese coverage uses イッポリート／キーサ・ヴォロビャニノフ; Chinese editions vary, 徐昌翰 (江苏凤凰文艺) gives 伊坡利·沃洛比亚尼诺夫 and the 2022 上海译文 edition (白桦熊) gives 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇, so 沃洛比亚尼诺夫/沃罗比亚尼诺夫 both circulate.

rendering.zh: 伊波利特·马特维耶维奇·沃罗比亚尼诺夫
rendering.ja: イッポリート・マトヴェーエヴィチ・ヴォロビャニノフ

Ипполит Матвеевич Воробьянинов.note_for_reader: Russians address adults formally by given name plus patronymic (father's name + -ovich/-evich); 'Ippolit Matveyevich' is respectful, and Bender's 'Kisa' ('Kitty') is a deliberately deflating childhood nickname.
Ипполит Матвеевич Воробьянинов.rationale: Full transliteration with the patronymic keeps the denotation and the formal, faintly antiquated register that name-and-patronymic carries; the class flavour of a Russian patronymic is not native to any target language and is supplied by a single note rather than by the name. Bender's epithets (Kisa, предводитель, патрон, фельдмаршал) are bound separately and are not folded into this rendering.

допр.finding: ДОПР = дом (общественно-)принудительных работ, 'house of forced labour': a Soviet penal institution of the 1920s, especially in the Ukrainian SSR (Ukr. БУПР), organised from 1920 and phased out with the 1929–30 shift to 'corrective-labour' camps and colonies; the Donetsk (Stalino) one, built for 120, held 542 in 1925. Commentaries to the novel gloss it as one variety of Soviet prison of the period, for sentences of roughly six months to two years for the 'not socially dangerous'. By 1928 it was a lower-case common noun in the Odessa/Ukraine speech Ilf and Petrov grew up with, meaning simply 'the clink'. In ch. VIII Ostap warns Pasha Emilevich: 'Один мой знакомый тоже продавал государственную мебель. Теперь он пошел в монахи — сидит в допре'; the joke is the substitution of 'taking monastic vows' (withdrawal from the world) for 'doing time', capped by the deflating slang word. The passage is absent from Richardson's 1961 English text (abridged), and I could not verify Fisher's 2011 rendering or the Chinese/Japanese editions online, so no established target rendering was found.

rendering.ja: 強制労働刑務所（ドプル）

допр.note_for_reader: ДОПР (dom prinuditelnykh rabot, 'house of forced labour'): a 1920s Soviet prison, chiefly in Ukraine; in everyday speech just 'jail'.
допр.rationale: All three keep the denotation (a prison, and specifically the NEP-era forced-labour prison, not a workhouse) and keep the monk-vs-prison joke, which lives in 'пошел в монахи — сидит' rather than in the acronym; kept the acronym in en and as a parenthetical in zh/ja so the side-by-side reader can match the Russian. Given up: the throwaway slang punch of a lower-case 'допр' and its Ukrainian-provincial colour, which no target-language word supplies without a note.

красный уголок.finding: A Soviet institution: a room or corner in every enterprise, school, barracks, dormitory or (as in ch. VIII of the novel) old people's home set aside for agitation and political education — Lenin portrait or bust, slogans, wall newspapers, pamphlets, newspaper readings, party/Komsomol meetings. Red corners appeared in the early 1920s out of literacy-campaign reading rooms and by the 1960s were mostly renamed 'Lenin rooms'. The name is a deliberate secular remake of the peasant 'красный угол' (the icon corner, 'beautiful corner') of every pre-revolutionary house, so for a 1928 reader it carried both the new-regime obligatoriness and the joke that the new religion had its own chapel; Russian sources note it has no Western-European equivalent. In the novel Alkhen's Starsobes has one, Ostap inspects it 'for fire safety', and Pasha Emilevich has sold the chair from it. Richardson's 1965 English translation flattens it to 'recreation room'; scholarship and popular English writing on Soviet culture use 'Red Corner' (sometimes 'Lenin corner'). Chinese coverage uses 红角 as the calque (with 上座/正座 for the older icon-corner sense); no established Japanese rendering was found, only calques like 赤いコーナー in general Soviet-culture material.

rendering.ja: 赤いコーナー

красный уголок.note_for_reader: Red Corner (красный уголок): the room every Soviet workplace kept for posters, newspapers and political meetings — the regime's replacement for the icon corner of the old peasant house.
красный уголок.rationale: Keeps denotation and the ironic connotation (a secular chapel, named after the icon corner) by binding the established calque in all three languages plus a one-time note; gives up self-explanatory transparency (Richardson's 'recreation room' reads instantly but erases the institution and the joke) and adds the parenthetical gloss 'political reading room' / 政治宣传室 / 政治学習室 only at first occurrence, not in the fixed term.

«Арагац».finding: «Арагац» appears in chapter XII (the parody 'Story of the Hussar-Hermit'): the hermit Evpl, sleeping in a coffin, first smears it with kerosene, then asks the old man to bring 'порошок «Арагац» против клопов' from town ('Но и «Арагац» не помог'), and finally tries the Glik brothers' pink liquid «Клопин» — a three-step escalation of NEP-era consumer remedies that all fail. The name is that of Mount Aragats, Armenia's highest peak; Armenian/Caucasian pyrethrum ('персидский порошок') was the standard insect powder, so a Caucasus-branded bug powder was plausible to a 1928 reader, but I could not confirm from an accessible source (Shcheglov's commentary is not online) whether «Арагац» was an actual product or an invented 'loud' NEP brand name like «Титаник» hair dye. The satirical point is that a grandly named product is useless, and the passage itself is a parody of anti-religious pamphlets. Richardson's 1961 English translation omits this chapter's inset story entirely; Anne O. Fisher's 2011 Northwestern edition (p. 151) renders it 'Aragats bedbug powder. But even the Aragats didn't help.' I found no accessible Chinese or Japanese rendering of the passage online.

rendering.ja: 南京虫駆除粉「アラガツ」

«Арагац».note_for_reader: Aragats: Armenia's highest mountain, used here as a brand name for a NEP-era insect powder.
«Арагац».rationale: Keeps the denotation (a branded, quoted product name, transliterated and matching Fisher's established 'Aragats') and the deadpan register of a real-sounding advertisement; gives up the connotation that a Russian reader caught unaided — the mountain name — which the one-line note restores at first occurrence. Use the same quoted brand form at every recurrence so the escalation kerosene → «Арагац» → «Клопин» stays visible.
